slides.title: What is money?
slides.text: Money is what we use to buy things we want or need — like a snack, a toy, or a book. For example, if you want a candy bar at the store, you hand the cashier some money, and they hand you the candy back.

slides.title: How do you get money?
slides.text: People earn money by working or doing helpful jobs — like completing chores! For example, if you help feed the dog or put away your toys every day this week, a grown-up might give you a coin for each job you finished.

slides.title: What does "saving" mean?
slides.text: Saving means keeping your money safe instead of spending it right away — like putting it in a piggy bank. For example, if you get 2 coins today and drop both into your piggy bank, they'll still be there tomorrow, and the day after that, safe and sound.

slides.title: Money can grow!
slides.text: If you plant a seed and water it, it slowly grows into a big plant. Saving works a little like that too — if you keep adding one coin every week, your pile of saved coins keeps getting bigger and bigger, even though you're not doing anything fancy, just adding a little at a time.

slides.title: What does "spending" mean?
slides.text: Spending is using your money to get something you want right now, like a toy or an ice cream. For example, if you have 3 coins and you use all 3 to buy a small toy car at the store, that's spending — you traded your coins for the toy you wanted.

slides.title: What is a store?
slides.text: A store is a place that sells things for money. For example, when you go to a grocery store with a grown-up, you might pick out an apple, the person at the counter tells you how many coins it costs, and you hand over the coins to take the apple home.

slides.title: You can share money too
slides.text: Sometimes people use money to help others — like buying a gift for a friend, or giving to someone who needs it. For example, if it's your friend's birthday, you might use some of your saved coins to buy them a small present, or drop a coin in a donation box to help someone who needs food.

slides.title: Waiting for something special
slides.text: Sometimes the thing you want costs more than you have right now. Saving up a little at a time until you have enough is worth the wait. For example, if a toy costs 10 coins but you only have 4, saving 2 more coins each week means that after just 3 weeks, you'd have enough to buy it!

slides.title: You get to choose!
slides.text: Every time you get money, you get to choose what to do with it: save it, spend it, or share it. There's no one right answer — it depends what you want most. For example, if you get 5 coins for your birthday, you might decide to save 2 for later, spend 2 on a treat today, and give 1 to your little brother.

slides.title: What is a bank?
slides.text: A bank is a safe place where people keep their money — like a giant, super-secure piggy bank. For example, instead of keeping 50 coins under your bed where they could get lost, a grown-up can put that money in a bank, and the bank keeps a careful record of exactly how much belongs to you.

slides.title: Saving for a goal
slides.text: Instead of spending money the moment you get it, you can save it up for something bigger you really want. For example, if a new bike costs $60 and you save $5 of your allowance every week, you'd have enough in about 12 weeks — a clear goal makes saving feel worth it.

slides.title: What is interest?
slides.text: Some banks pay you a little extra money just for keeping your savings there. That extra bit is called interest — a small reward for saving. For example, if a bank pays you 5 cents of interest for every $1 you keep saved for a whole year, then $20 saved could turn into $21 without you doing anything extra at all.

slides.title: Wants vs. needs
slides.text: A need is something you must have, like food. A want is something nice to have, like a video game. Knowing the difference helps you spend wisely. For example, new shoes when yours are falling apart is a need, but a third pair of sneakers just because you like the color is a want.

slides.title: Making a simple budget
slides.text: A budget is just a plan for your money — deciding ahead of time how much you'll save, spend, and maybe share, before you actually get it. For example, if you get $10 for your birthday, a simple budget might be: $5 into savings, $3 to spend on something fun now, and $2 to share or give to someone else.

slides.title: Patience pays off
slides.text: Waiting a little longer before buying something — instead of grabbing it right away — often means you can afford something even better later. For example, spending all $8 on a small toy today feels fun, but waiting three more weeks might mean you can afford the bigger toy you actually wanted most.

slides.title: Comparing prices
slides.text: Smart shoppers check if the same thing costs less somewhere else before buying it. A few minutes of comparing can save a lot of points or money. For example, if the same toy costs $12 at one store and $9 at another, checking both stores first could save you $3 to spend on something else.

slides.title: Setting a savings goal
slides.text: Picking one specific thing to save for — and figuring out how many weeks of saving it'll take — makes saving feel a lot more real and exciting. For example, saving $2 a week toward a $16 game means marking off each week on a calendar until, after week 8, you finally have enough.

slides.title: What is a bank account?
slides.text: A bank account is like a digital piggy bank — the bank keeps track of exactly how much money you have, and you can check the balance any time. For example, instead of counting coins yourself, a bank statement might simply say "balance: $37" so you always know where you stand.

slides.title: Watching your savings add up
slides.text: Writing down how much you've saved each week and adding it up is a simple way to actually see your money growing toward a goal. For example, keeping a little chart that goes $2, $4, $6, $8 each week turns saving into something you can watch happen, instead of just hoping it's working.

slides.title: What is investing?
slides.text: Investing means using your money to buy a small piece of something — like a company — hoping it grows in value over time. For example, if you use $50 to buy a small piece of a company that makes sneakers, and more people start buying those sneakers, your $50 piece could grow to be worth $60 or more.

slides.title: What is a stock?
slides.text: A stock is a tiny piece of ownership in a company. If the company does well, your tiny piece can become worth more. For example, if a company that makes your favorite video game has 1,000 total pieces (stocks) and you own 1 of them, you technically own a tiny 1/1000th sliver of that whole company.

slides.title: Risk and reward
slides.text: Investments can go up AND down in value. Taking on some risk is part of how investing can lead to bigger rewards over time. For example, $100 invested might grow to $110 in a good year, but it could also drop to $90 in a rough year before recovering later — that up-and-down ride is the risk part of the deal.

slides.title: The power of time
slides.text: The earlier you start investing — even with a small amount — the more time your money has to grow. Time is a young investor's biggest advantage. For example, $100 invested at age 12 has decades to grow before retirement, while the same $100 invested at age 40 has far less time to do the same job.

slides.title: What is compound interest?
slides.text: Compound interest means you earn money not just on what you put in, but also on the money it already earned before. It's growth building on growth. For example, $100 growing by 10% becomes $110 after year one — then in year two, that 10% growth applies to the full $110, not just your original $100, making $121.

slides.title: Short-term vs. long-term goals
slides.text: Money you need soon (like next month) is usually better off saved, not invested. Money you won't need for many years has more room to ride out an investment's ups and downs. For example, money for a video game you want to buy next month should stay in simple savings, while money you won't touch for 5+ years has time to recover from any dips.

slides.title: What is a "loss"?
slides.text: Sometimes an investment's value drops for a while — that's a loss on paper. It only becomes a real loss if you sell while it's down instead of waiting for it to recover. For example, if your $100 investment drops to $80 but you leave it alone and it climbs back to $105 a year later, you never actually lost anything — the dip was only temporary.

slides.title: Investing vs. an allowance
slides.text: An allowance is money you're simply given. Investing is different — it's money you put to work, hoping it grows into more than you started with. For example, a $10 weekly allowance stays $10 no matter what, but $10 invested wisely could grow to be worth $12, $15, or more over several years.

slides.title: Investing a little, regularly
slides.text: Instead of investing one big amount all at once, some people invest a smaller amount on a regular schedule — like monthly. This is sometimes called dollar-cost averaging, and it smooths out the ups and downs. For example, investing $10 every month for a year means some months you buy when prices are higher and some when they're lower, which balances out instead of betting everything on one moment.

slides.title: What is a brokerage account?
slides.text: A brokerage account is where you actually buy and hold investments like stocks — different from a regular bank account, which just holds cash. For example, a parent might open a custodial brokerage account for a young teen, where the teen can pick which companies to invest small amounts in, with a parent supervising.

slides.title: Don't put all your eggs in one basket
slides.text: Diversification means spreading your money across many different investments instead of just one, so one bad outcome doesn't wipe you out. For example, investing $500 entirely in one company means you're in trouble if that company struggles, but spreading it across 100 different companies means one bad one barely dents your total.

slides.title: What is an index fund?
slides.text: Instead of picking one company, an index fund lets you own a tiny piece of hundreds of companies at once — an easy way to diversify. For example, a single index fund investment might give you a small stake in 500 of the largest companies in the country, all through one simple purchase instead of researching and buying 500 stocks yourself.

slides.title: Inflation: the silent thief
slides.text: Prices tend to rise over time. Money that just sits still loses buying power. Investing is one way to try to grow money faster than inflation shrinks it. For example, if a candy bar costs $1 today and prices rise 3% a year, that same candy bar could cost about $1.34 in ten years — meaning $100 sitting in cash quietly buys less and less over time.

slides.title: Long-term thinking beats quick wins
slides.text: Investors who stay patient through ups and downs, over years or decades, tend to do far better than those chasing quick trades. For example, someone who invested $1,000 and left it alone for 20 years, riding out several rough patches, has historically ended up far ahead of someone who panic-sold every time prices dipped.

slides.title: Debt works the opposite way
slides.text: Investing grows money for you over time. Borrowing money (debt) usually costs you extra over time through interest — it's compounding working against you instead of for you. For example, a $200 credit card balance charging 20% interest a year can balloon if left unpaid, the same way compound growth builds up an investment — just in the wrong direction.

slides.title: Retirement accounts, simplified
slides.text: Many workplaces offer special accounts (like a 401(k) or an IRA in the US) built for long-term investing, often with tax advantages. They're designed to be left alone for decades. For example, some employers even match part of what you put in — meaning if you contribute $50, your employer might add another $25 for free, instantly growing your investment.

slides.title: Getting started today
slides.text: Modern investing apps and custodial accounts have made it easier than ever for a teenager to start investing small, real amounts with a parent's help. For example, a 16-year-old could start with just $20 in a custodial brokerage account, buying a small stake in an index fund and adding a bit more each month.

slides.title: The Rule of 72
slides.text: A quick trick: divide 72 by your investment's yearly growth rate to estimate how many years it takes to double. At 8% growth, that's roughly 72 ÷ 8 = 9 years to double. For example, $500 growing at 8% a year would roughly become $1,000 after about 9 years, and roughly $2,000 after about 18 years.

slides.title: Bull markets and bear markets
slides.text: A 'bull market' is a stretch of time when prices are generally rising. A 'bear market' is a stretch when prices are generally falling. Both are completely normal parts of a long investing journey. For example, markets have historically gone through both bull and bear stretches many times over the decades, and investors who stayed invested through both tended to come out ahead in the long run.

slides.title: A brief word on taxes
slides.text: In many places, profit made from selling an investment can be taxed — often called a capital gains tax. It's a real cost worth knowing about, even though the details vary a lot by country. For example, if you bought a stock for $100 and sold it for $150, that $50 profit might be taxed, meaning your actual take-home gain would be a bit less than $50.

slides.title: Meet AI!
slides.text: AI is a computer helper. It can listen to you and talk back — kind of like a friendly robot voice. For example, you might say "what's the weather today?" out loud, and a smart speaker answers you right back, almost like talking to a friend.

slides.title: Ask it something!
slides.text: Some speakers and toys can answer your questions or play your favorite song when you ask them out loud. For example, saying "play my favorite song" to a smart speaker can make music start playing almost instantly, without anyone pressing a single button.

slides.title: A person built it
slides.text: AI doesn't just appear out of nowhere — clever people built it to help us, just like someone built your favorite toy. For example, a team of people spent a long time writing instructions and testing a talking toy robot before it ever ended up on a store shelf.

slides.title: AI doesn't have real feelings
slides.text: Even when AI talks in a friendly voice, it can't really feel happy, sad, or love you the way a person or a pet can. For example, if you tell an AI toy "I love you," it might say something nice back, but it doesn't actually feel love the way your mom, dad, or dog does.

slides.title: AI can help make things
slides.text: Some AI can help draw a silly picture or make up a story when you ask it to — like a helper for making fun stuff. For example, you could ask an AI to "draw a purple dinosaur eating pizza," and it can create a picture matching exactly that, in just a few seconds.

slides.title: AI isn't always right
slides.text: Sometimes AI gets confused and gives a silly or wrong answer — it's still learning, just like you are! For example, you might ask an AI toy what 2 plus 2 is, and every once in a while it gets mixed up and says the wrong number — just like you might sometimes make a mistake too.

slides.title: AI can make music too
slides.text: Some AI can put sounds together to make a little tune, kind of like how it can help draw a picture. For example, you could ask an AI to "make a happy song about a kitten," and it could put together a short little tune just for that.

slides.title: AI shows up in surprising places
slides.text: AI can help some toy cars drive themselves around a track, or help a game character know where to move next. For example, a remote-control car with AI built in might be able to notice a wall coming up and steer around it all by itself, without you pressing any buttons.

slides.title: Ask a grown-up first
slides.text: If you want to use an AI toy or app, or you're not sure about something it says, always check with a grown-up first. For example, if an AI toy tells you something confusing or says to do something unusual, checking with a parent before following it is always the safe choice.

slides.title: AI learns from examples
slides.text: Instead of being told exact rules, AI often learns by looking at thousands (or millions!) of examples and finding patterns in them. For example, to learn what a cat looks like, an AI might be shown a million different pictures of cats until it starts noticing what they all have in common.

slides.title: Where you already see AI
slides.text: Video game characters that react to you, apps that recommend videos you might like, and voice assistants all use AI. For example, if you've ever noticed a video app suggesting "you might also like" a video right after you finished watching one, that suggestion came from AI noticing a pattern in what you watched.

slides.title: Finding patterns
slides.text: If AI sees enough pictures of dogs, it starts noticing patterns — like "dogs usually have four legs and fur" — and uses that to guess. For example, after seeing thousands of dog photos, an AI might correctly guess that a new, unfamiliar photo is a dog because it has four legs, fur, and floppy ears, matching the pattern it learned.

slides.title: AI can make mistakes
slides.text: Because AI learns from patterns, it can sometimes get things wrong — especially with something unusual it hasn't seen much before. For example, an AI trained mostly on photos of fluffy dogs might mistakenly guess that a fluffy sheep in a photo is also a dog, since it looks similar to the pattern it learned.

slides.title: AI vs. your brain
slides.text: Your brain can understand feelings, come up with brand-new ideas, and truly care about people. AI is very good at specific tasks, but it doesn't understand things the way you do. For example, an AI can recognize a sad face in a photo, but it doesn't actually feel sad or worry about the person the way a friend would.

slides.title: Being a smart AI user
slides.text: Just because AI says something doesn't mean it's true. Smart AI users double-check important information instead of believing everything right away. For example, if an AI tells you an animal fact that sounds surprising, checking it in a book or asking a grown-up before repeating it as true is a smart habit.

slides.title: Robots vs. AI
slides.text: A robot is a physical machine. AI is the 'smart' software that can control a robot — or can run inside a phone or computer with no robot body at all. For example, a voice assistant on a phone is AI with no robot body at all, while a robot vacuum uses AI to decide where to move, inside an actual physical machine.

slides.title: AI helps you search
slides.text: When you search for something online, AI often helps decide which results are most likely to actually answer your question. For example, if you search "how tall is a giraffe," AI helps pick out the most useful answer from millions of possible web pages, instead of just showing them in a random order.

slides.title: People see AI differently
slides.text: Some people are really excited about AI and what it can do. Others feel worried about it. Both views are worth listening to — AI is still a new, changing technology. For example, a scientist might be excited that AI can help discover new medicines, while someone else might worry about AI toys not knowing when to say the right thing.

slides.title: Training data
slides.text: AI systems are "trained" on huge amounts of data — text, images, or numbers — that teach the AI the patterns it's meant to learn. For example, a language-translation AI might be trained on millions of sentences that have already been translated by humans, learning from all of those examples how one language maps to another.

slides.title: Prediction, not real understanding
slides.text: Many AI tools, like chatbots, work by predicting the most likely next word or answer based on patterns — not by truly understanding meaning the way a person does. For example, when you type "the capital of France is," a chatbot predicts "Paris" is the most likely next word based on patterns in text it's seen, not because it understands geography the way a person does.

slides.title: AI can be biased
slides.text: If the data used to train an AI contains unfair patterns, the AI can repeat those unfair patterns too. This is called bias, and it's a real challenge engineers work hard to fix. For example, an AI trained mostly on photos of one type of job worker might wrongly assume that job is always done by one kind of person, simply because that's what most of its training photos showed.

slides.title: Generative AI
slides.text: Some AI can create brand-new text, images, or music by combining patterns it learned — this is called generative AI, and it powers many chatbots and art generators. For example, typing "a cat wearing a space suit, painted like a Renaissance portrait" into an image generator can produce a picture nobody has ever drawn before, built entirely from patterns the AI learned.

slides.title: AI and privacy
slides.text: AI tools often need data to work well. Being thoughtful about what personal information you share with an AI app matters, just like with any app. For example, telling an AI chatbot your full name, school, and home address isn't necessary to get help with homework, and that kind of detail is best kept private.

slides.title: Fact-checking AI answers
slides.text: AI can sound very confident even when it's wrong — sometimes called a "hallucination." Always double-check important facts from a trusted source. For example, an AI might confidently state a made-up historical date or invent a fake book title that sounds completely real, so checking a surprising fact against an encyclopedia or trusted website is a smart habit.

slides.title: AI's growing role
slides.text: AI already helps translate languages, spot diseases in medical scans, and recommend what you watch or read — and its role keeps growing. For example, some hospitals use AI to help doctors spot early signs of illness in X-rays faster than checking every scan by hand alone.

slides.title: AI working with people
slides.text: In many fields, AI is a tool that works alongside a person — helping a doctor spot something on a scan faster, for example — rather than fully replacing their judgment. For example, an AI might flag a spot on a medical scan as "worth a closer look," but a trained doctor still makes the final decision about what it means and what to do next.

slides.title: AI keeps changing
slides.text: AI systems get updated and retrained over time, so an AI tool from a year ago might behave quite differently — hopefully better — today. For example, an AI chatbot that struggled with math problems a year ago might handle the exact same questions correctly today, after being retrained on more examples.

slides.title: Neural networks, simplified
slides.text: Many modern AI systems are loosely inspired by how brain cells connect — layers of simple math functions combining to recognize very complex patterns. For example, one layer of a neural network might notice simple edges in a photo, the next layer combines edges into shapes like an eye or an ear, and a later layer combines those shapes to recognize an entire face.

slides.title: Large language models
slides.text: Chatbots you may have used are often "large language models" trained on enormous amounts of text to predict likely, coherent responses. For example, a large language model trained on huge amounts of internet text, books, and articles can write a coherent paragraph about almost any topic by predicting, word by word, what's most likely to come next.

slides.title: Bias and fairness
slides.text: Because AI learns from real-world data, it can inherit real-world unfairness, like reflecting stereotypes. Researchers actively study how to detect and reduce this. For example, a hiring AI trained on a company's past hiring decisions could accidentally learn and repeat past unfair patterns, like favoring one group over another, unless researchers specifically test for and correct that.

slides.title: Deepfakes and misinformation
slides.text: AI can now generate very convincing fake images, video, or audio. Learning to question what you see online is a genuinely important skill now. For example, a fake video could show a celebrity or politician appearing to say something they never actually said, convincing enough that many viewers wouldn't realize it was generated by AI.

slides.title: AI and jobs
slides.text: AI is changing many jobs — automating some repetitive tasks while creating new kinds of work. Understanding AI, rather than fearing it, is a real advantage for your future. For example, AI can now handle repetitive data entry tasks that used to take a person hours, while at the same time creating entirely new jobs like training and supervising AI systems.

slides.title: Using AI responsibly for school
slides.text: AI can be a great study partner for explaining concepts, but relying on it to do your thinking for you weakens the exact skills you're in school to build. For example, asking an AI to explain a tricky math concept in a different way, then solving practice problems yourself, builds real understanding — but asking it to just write your entire essay for you does not.

slides.title: Data and consent
slides.text: Many AI systems are trained on massive datasets pulled from the internet, which raises real questions about consent and ownership that society is still working out. For example, an AI image generator trained on millions of artists' work online raises the question of whether those artists should have been asked first, or compensated, for their work being used that way.

slides.title: Why understanding AI matters for you
slides.text: Whatever career you choose, AI will likely touch it. Understanding the basics now — not just using AI, but roughly how it works and where it fails — is a genuine head start. For example, a future doctor, lawyer, or artist who understands both the strengths and blind spots of AI tools will likely use them far more effectively than someone who either avoids them entirely or trusts them blindly.

slides.title: AI and energy use
slides.text: Training very large AI models takes a significant amount of computing power and electricity — an environmental cost that researchers and companies are actively working to reduce. For example, training one very large language model can use as much electricity as hundreds of homes use in a year, which is why more efficient training methods are an active area of research.

slides.title: New rules for AI
slides.text: Governments around the world are starting to write laws and regulations about how AI can be built and used — an evolving area, similar to how early internet and privacy laws once developed. For example, some regions now require companies to clearly label AI-generated content or disclose when a chatbot, not a human, is responding to a customer.

slides.title: What is a lemonade stand?
slides.text: A lemonade stand is a tiny business — you make something (lemonade!) and sell it to people who want to buy it. For example, on a hot day you might set up a little table outside with a pitcher of lemonade and a sign, and neighbors walking by can stop and buy a cup.

slides.title: What is trading?
slides.text: Trading means giving someone something they want, and getting something you want back — like a coin for a cup of lemonade. For example, your neighbor gives you a coin, and you give them a cold cup of lemonade in return — both of you end up happy with the trade.

slides.title: Where ideas come from
slides.text: A business often starts with a simple idea — like noticing people get thirsty and thinking, 'I could sell them a cold drink!' For example, if you notice people walking their dogs past your house every morning looking tired and hot, that's exactly the kind of noticing that could turn into a lemonade stand idea.

slides.title: Who is a customer?
slides.text: A customer is someone who buys what you're selling. Being friendly and helpful makes customers want to come back. For example, if you smile and say "thank you, have a great day!" to everyone who buys lemonade, they're much more likely to stop by your stand again next time.

slides.title: You can make things too!
slides.text: Drawing pictures, making bracelets, or baking cookies to share or sell are all little ways of being an entrepreneur — someone who makes and offers things. For example, if you make friendship bracelets and a few classmates want to trade a small toy or a coin for one, you're already being a little entrepreneur.

slides.title: It takes effort
slides.text: Making a lemonade stand work takes real effort — squeezing lemons, making a sign, and standing there smiling at customers! For example, before you sell a single cup, you might spend 20 minutes squeezing lemons, another 10 minutes making a colorful sign, and then stand outside for an hour waiting for customers to come by.

slides.title: Making something to sell
slides.text: Before you can sell something, you have to make it first — like squeezing the lemons and mixing in sugar and water to actually make the lemonade. For example, you can't sell a single cup of lemonade until you've actually squeezed the lemons, added sugar and water, and stirred it all together first.

slides.title: A happy customer comes back
slides.text: When a customer really likes what you sold them, they often want to come back and buy from you again. For example, if your neighbor loves your lemonade so much that they tell you "that was the best lemonade I've ever had," chances are they'll stop by again the next time you open your stand.

slides.title: Spotting a problem to solve
slides.text: Good business ideas often start by spotting a problem — like 'nobody sells cold water at the park' — and figuring out how to fix it. For example, if you notice that kids playing soccer at the park have nowhere nearby to buy a cold drink on a hot day, that gap is exactly the kind of problem a small business could solve.

slides.title: Cost vs. price
slides.text: Cost is what it takes to make something (like lemons and sugar). Price is what you charge someone to buy it. The difference is your profit. For example, if a cup of lemonade costs you 20 cents to make (lemons, sugar, and a cup) and you sell it for $1, your profit on that one cup is 80 cents.

slides.title: A simple plan
slides.text: Before starting, it helps to plan: what will you sell, how much will it cost to make, and how much will you charge? For example, a simple plan might say: "I'll sell lemonade, it costs 20 cents a cup to make, and I'll charge $1 a cup" — writing that down before you start avoids confusion later.

slides.title: Good customer service
slides.text: Being friendly, honest, and helpful makes people want to buy from you again — and tell their friends about you too. For example, if a customer asks for less sugar in their lemonade and you happily make it exactly how they like it, they're likely to become a repeat customer and mention your stand to others.

slides.title: Telling people about it
slides.text: Even a great product needs people to know it exists! A colorful sign or telling your neighbors is a simple form of marketing. For example, making a bright poster that says "Cold Lemonade — $1!" and putting it where people walking by can see it is a simple way to let people know your stand exists.

slides.title: Keeping track
slides.text: Writing down what you spent and what you earned helps you see if your little business is actually making money. For example, if you write down "spent $4 on lemons and sugar, earned $12 selling cups," you can quickly see you made an $8 profit for the day.

slides.title: Trying again if it doesn't work
slides.text: If a business idea doesn't work the first time, entrepreneurs often tweak it and try again instead of giving up. For example, if nobody stopped at your lemonade stand on a cloudy day, you might try moving to a sunnier spot or adding a fun new flavor next time instead of giving up on the idea completely.

slides.title: Making your product special
slides.text: Adding something unique — like a fun flavor of lemonade nobody else has — can make customers pick your stand over anyone else's. For example, adding a splash of strawberry or mint to your lemonade, something the other kids' stands down the street don't offer, could be exactly why customers choose your stand.

slides.title: Planning your day
slides.text: Deciding when to open your stand, how much lemonade to make, and what supplies you need ahead of time helps the whole day run more smoothly. For example, deciding the night before to open from 2-4pm, make one full pitcher, and bring 20 cups means you won't be scrambling to figure things out once customers start showing up.

slides.title: Profit and loss
slides.text: If you earn more than you spend, that's a profit. If you spend more than you earn, that's a loss. Tracking both helps a business survive. For example, if your dog-walking side business earns $60 in a month but spent $75 on flyers, leashes, and treats, that month was actually a $15 loss, even though $60 sounds like good money.

slides.title: Knowing your customer
slides.text: Successful businesses understand who they're selling to — what that person likes, needs, and is willing to pay for. For example, if you're selling handmade bookmarks, knowing that your customers are mostly classmates who love a specific book series could help you design bookmarks featuring those characters, which they'd be far more excited to buy.

slides.title: Teamwork in business
slides.text: Many businesses run better with a team — different people handling different jobs, like making the product, selling it, and managing money. For example, if you and a friend start a dog-walking business together, one of you could focus on finding new customers while the other tracks the schedule and money — splitting the work makes it easier to grow.

slides.title: Taking a smart risk
slides.text: Starting a business always involves some risk — it might not work. Smart entrepreneurs take risks they can afford, not risks that could ruin them. For example, spending $10 of your own savings to try selling friendship bracelets at a school fair is a smart, affordable risk — spending your entire year's savings on the same idea would not be.

slides.title: Reinvesting in growth
slides.text: Instead of spending all the profit right away, many entrepreneurs put some of it back into the business — better supplies, a nicer sign, more inventory. For example, if your bracelet business earns $20 profit one week, using $10 of it to buy more beads and string for next week (instead of spending it all on yourself) helps the business keep growing.

slides.title: Standing out from competitors
slides.text: If other people sell something similar, a business needs a reason customers should pick them — better quality, price, or service. For example, if three kids at your school are all selling friendship bracelets, offering custom colors made to order, or slightly better prices, gives customers a specific reason to choose you.

slides.title: Word of mouth
slides.text: Happy customers telling their friends is one of the most powerful (and free!) ways a small business grows. For example, if one classmate loves the bracelet you made them and shows five friends at lunch, you might suddenly have five new customers without spending a single cent on advertising.

slides.title: Building a name people remember
slides.text: A consistent name, look, or feel for your business — sometimes called a brand — helps customers recognize and trust you again next time. For example, always using the same logo sticker and the same colorful packaging for your bracelets helps customers instantly recognize "oh, that's from her bracelet business" when they see it.

slides.title: Selling online with help
slides.text: With a parent's help, some young entrepreneurs sell crafts or art through simple online marketplaces, reaching far more people than a stand on the street. For example, a 12-year-old who makes custom drawings might, with a parent's account and supervision, list a few pieces online and reach buyers far beyond just their own neighborhood.

slides.title: What is a business plan?
slides.text: A business plan lays out what a business will sell, who it's for, how it'll make money, and what it needs to get started — a roadmap for turning an idea into reality. For example, a teen wanting to start a pet-sitting business might write a one-page plan covering who their customers are (nearby pet owners), how much they'll charge per visit, and what supplies (a leash, treats, a scheduling app) they need first.

slides.title: Startup vs. small business
slides.text: A small business often grows steadily and stays similar in size. A startup usually aims to grow very fast, often testing a new idea that hasn't been proven yet. For example, a local pet-sitting business run by one teen is a small business, growing steadily one customer at a time — while an app trying to connect thousands of pet owners with sitters nationwide, aiming to grow fast, would be more like a startup.

slides.title: Where funding comes from
slides.text: Businesses can be funded with personal savings, loans, or investors who give money in exchange for a share of future profits or ownership. For example, a teen might use $50 of their own savings to buy initial supplies, while a bigger startup might convince an investor to provide $50,000 in exchange for owning 10% of the company.

slides.title: What does "scaling" mean?
slides.text: Scaling means growing a business to serve many more customers without everything becoming proportionally more expensive or difficult to manage. For example, a tutoring business that only earns more by adding more of the tutor's own hours doesn't scale well, but selling a recorded video course that hundreds of students can buy without extra work per student scales much better.

slides.title: Failure is part of the process
slides.text: Many successful entrepreneurs failed at a first (or second, or third) attempt. Learning from what went wrong is often what makes the next attempt succeed. For example, a teen's first attempt at selling custom phone cases online might flop due to poor photos and unclear pricing — but applying those exact lessons to a second attempt often leads to real success.

slides.title: Ethics in business
slides.text: Long-term success usually depends on being honest with customers, treating employees fairly, and not cutting corners just to make a quick profit. For example, honestly describing a product's condition, even when a vague description might sell it faster, builds the kind of trust that keeps customers coming back for years.

slides.title: Solving a real problem
slides.text: The most durable businesses tend to solve a genuine problem for people — not just chase a trend that might fade quickly. For example, a tutoring business solving a real, ongoing need (students struggling with math) tends to last far longer than a business built around a fad that's popular for a few months and then forgotten.

slides.title: Resilience and persistence
slides.text: Markets change, plans fail, and competitors appear. Entrepreneurs who adapt and keep going tend to outlast those who give up at the first setback. For example, if a new competitor undercuts your prices, adapting by improving your service or finding a new customer niche is more likely to succeed than simply giving up.

slides.title: Businesses that also help others
slides.text: Some entrepreneurs build 'social enterprises' — businesses designed to make money while also solving a social or environmental problem, not purely for profit. For example, a teen-run business that sells reusable water bottles and donates a portion of every sale to a clean-water charity is pursuing both profit and positive impact at the same time.

slides.title: Measuring success beyond money
slides.text: Revenue matters, but many entrepreneurs also track customer satisfaction, repeat business, and real-world impact as signs their business is genuinely succeeding. For example, a business that earns a modest profit but has 90% of customers coming back again and again is arguably in a stronger position than one earning more but constantly losing and replacing one-time customers.

slides.title: Why do we ask "why"?
slides.text: Asking 'why' helps you understand things better — like why the sky looks blue, or why ice melts in the sun. For example, if you ask "why does ice melt?" and learn that warmth turns ice back into water, you'll understand something new every time you see ice cubes melting in a cup.

slides.title: Same or different?
slides.text: Looking closely at two things and noticing how they're the same or different is a great thinking skill — like comparing two toys. For example, comparing a red rubber ball and a red balloon, you might notice they're both red and round, but one bounces and the other pops — noticing those details is real thinking.

slides.title: Real or pretend?
slides.text: A cartoon dragon breathing fire is pretend. A real dog barking is real. Telling the difference is an important thinking skill. For example, if you see a talking cat on TV, you can think "that's pretend, cats can't really talk" — while a real cat meowing next to you is really happening.

slides.title: Think before you act
slides.text: Taking a moment to think before doing something — like before grabbing a toy from a friend — often leads to a better choice. For example, instead of grabbing a toy your friend is using, pausing for a second to think "I could ask if I can play too" usually leads to a happier outcome for both of you.

slides.title: Looking for clues
slides.text: If your shoes are wet, you can think about clues to figure out why — did it rain? Did you step in a puddle? For example, if you look outside and see puddles on the ground, that clue helps explain why your shoes got wet during your walk.

slides.title: It's okay to ask questions
slides.text: If something doesn't make sense, asking a question is smart — not silly. Good thinkers ask lots of questions. For example, if a teacher explains something and you're not sure you understood, raising your hand and asking "can you explain that again?" is exactly what a good thinker does.

slides.title: Sorting things into groups
slides.text: Putting toys into groups — like all the red ones together, or all the round ones together — is a first step toward organized thinking. For example, sorting a pile of mixed toys into "cars," "animals," and "blocks" helps you see patterns and find what you're looking for much faster later.

slides.title: What comes next?
slides.text: Looking at a pattern like circle, square, circle, square and figuring out what comes next is a fun way to practice thinking ahead. For example, if you see the pattern red, blue, red, blue, red, you can predict the next color should be blue, because that's the pattern repeating.

slides.title: Fact vs. opinion
slides.text: A fact is something that's true and can be checked, like 'the sun is hot.' An opinion is what someone thinks or feels, like 'summer is the best season.' For example, "the movie is 90 minutes long" is a fact you could check with a clock, while "the movie was boring" is just one person's opinion — someone else might feel completely differently.

slides.title: Asking good questions
slides.text: Instead of just accepting an answer, good thinkers ask follow-up questions like 'how do you know that?' or 'is there another way to look at this?' For example, if a friend says "this game is the best one ever," asking "what makes it the best?" helps you understand their reasoning instead of just taking their word for it.

slides.title: More than one answer
slides.text: Some questions have more than one reasonable answer. Thinking about different possibilities, not just the first idea, leads to better decisions. For example, if you're deciding how to spend a free afternoon, there might be several good options — reading, playing outside, or building something — and thinking through more than one before choosing usually leads to a happier choice.

slides.title: Don't believe everything right away
slides.text: Just because something is written down, said out loud, or shown online doesn't automatically make it true. For example, a video claiming "this trick will make you super strong instantly" sounds exciting, but just because it's posted online doesn't mean it's actually true.

slides.title: Checking with a trusted source
slides.text: If you're not sure whether something is true, checking with a grown-up, a book, or a trusted website is a smart next step. For example, if a friend tells you a surprising animal fact, like "elephants can't jump," checking it in a nature book or asking a grown-up confirms whether it's actually true.

slides.title: Cause and effect
slides.text: Thinking about why something happened — the cause — and what happened because of it — the effect — helps you understand the world more clearly. For example, if you forgot to water a plant (the cause) and it wilted a few days later (the effect), understanding that connection helps you remember to water it next time.

slides.title: Changing your mind
slides.text: If new information shows your first idea was wrong, a good thinker isn't afraid to change their mind. For example, if you thought a certain animal was a reptile, but then learn it's actually a mammal, updating what you believe based on the new fact is exactly what a strong thinker does.

slides.title: Being a detective
slides.text: A good detective gathers several clues before deciding what happened, instead of guessing after just one clue. Thinking works the same way. For example, if a plant is dying, a good detective-thinker would check multiple clues — sunlight, water, soil — instead of assuming it's just one thing after a quick glance.

slides.title: It's okay to disagree
slides.text: Two people can look at the same thing and see it differently. Disagreeing with a friend — respectfully — doesn't mean the friendship is in trouble. For example, you might think a book's ending was happy while your friend thinks it was sad — you can both explain your reasoning and still be great friends.

slides.title: Evaluating evidence
slides.text: Before believing a claim, it helps to ask: what evidence supports it? Is the evidence strong, weak, or missing entirely? For example, if a classmate claims "this energy drink makes you smarter," asking what actual studies or evidence back that up — versus just a company's advertisement — helps you judge whether it's really true.

slides.title: Spotting assumptions
slides.text: An assumption is something believed without proof. Noticing hidden assumptions in an argument helps you judge whether it actually holds up. For example, the argument "he must be good at math because he's Asian" hides an unproven assumption about a whole group of people, which makes the argument weak the moment you notice it.

slides.title: Correlation isn't causation
slides.text: Just because two things happen around the same time doesn't mean one caused the other. Ice cream sales and sunburns both rise in summer — but ice cream doesn't cause sunburn. For example, if students who play a certain video game also tend to get good grades, that doesn't necessarily mean the game caused the good grades — maybe both are just linked to having more free time at home.

slides.title: Considering other perspectives
slides.text: Understanding how a situation looks from someone else's point of view often reveals things your own perspective alone would miss. For example, a disagreement between two group project members might look totally different once you understand that one person was juggling other responsibilities the other didn't know about.

slides.title: Weighing both sides
slides.text: On a genuinely debatable topic, looking fairly at the strongest arguments on both sides — before forming an opinion — leads to more solid conclusions. For example, before deciding your opinion on whether school should start later, actually reading the strongest arguments on both sides — about sleep and about schedules — leads to a more solid opinion than just picking a side because it sounds nice.

slides.title: Defining the real problem
slides.text: Sometimes what looks like the problem is actually just a symptom of a different, deeper problem. Defining the real issue is the first step to solving it well. For example, a student who keeps falling asleep in class might seem lazy, but the real problem could be staying up too late — fixing bedtime, not "trying harder to stay awake," is what actually solves it.

slides.title: Checking the source
slides.text: Who is saying this, and why? A source with something to gain from you believing a claim deserves a closer, more careful look. For example, an ad for a supplement claiming it "boosts brainpower" comes from a company that profits if you believe it — which is exactly why it deserves more scrutiny than a neutral science article on the same topic.

slides.title: Setting a goal and checking progress
slides.text: Deciding what you're aiming for, then regularly checking whether your approach is actually getting you closer, keeps effort from being wasted. For example, if your goal is to improve a test score, checking after a few practice tests whether your study method is actually helping lets you switch strategies early instead of wasting weeks on something that isn't working.

slides.title: Averages can mislead
slides.text: An average can hide a lot — a class 'average score' of 75% might mean everyone scored near 75%, or it might mean half scored 100% and half scored 50%. For example, two classes could both report a 75% average test score, but one class might have every student scoring close to 75%, while the other has half the class acing it and half failing badly — very different situations hidden behind the same number.

slides.title: What is confirmation bias?
slides.text: Confirmation bias is the tendency to notice and believe information that agrees with what you already think, while ignoring information that doesn't. For example, someone convinced a certain diet is unhealthy might notice and remember every negative story about it, while barely registering the many studies showing it's fine — without even realizing they're doing it.

slides.title: Media literacy
slides.text: Understanding who created a piece of media, why, and who it's meant to persuade helps you judge how much to trust it. For example, an article about a product's benefits written by the company that sells it deserves a different level of trust than an independent review with no financial stake in the outcome.

slides.title: Common logical fallacies
slides.text: A logical fallacy is a flaw in reasoning — like attacking a person instead of their argument, or assuming something is true just because 'everyone believes it.' For example, responding to someone's argument about climate policy by saying "well, you're not even a scientist" attacks the person instead of addressing what they actually said — that's a logical fallacy, not a real rebuttal.

slides.title: Weighing evidence fairly
slides.text: Strong critical thinkers weigh the quality and quantity of evidence on all sides before forming a conclusion — not just picking whichever side feels more comfortable. For example, when researching a controversial topic for a school paper, deliberately reading strong arguments on both sides, not just the ones that confirm what you already believed, produces a far more credible paper.

slides.title: Deciding under uncertainty
slides.text: Many real decisions have to be made without knowing everything for certain. Thinking in terms of likely outcomes, not guaranteed ones, leads to better choices. For example, choosing a college major isn't about finding a guaranteed-perfect choice — it's about weighing which path seems most likely to lead somewhere you'd be happy, given what you know now.

slides.title: Being willing to update
slides.text: Genuinely strong thinkers treat their own conclusions as open to revision — new, credible evidence should be able to change a well-reasoned mind. For example, if you strongly believed a certain study supported your view, but later learned that study was retracted for bad data, updating your opinion in light of that is a sign of strength, not weakness.

slides.title: Steelmanning an argument
slides.text: Instead of attacking the weakest version of an opposing view, a strong thinker engages with the strongest, most reasonable version of it — called 'steelmanning.' For example, instead of arguing against the silliest version of an opposing political view you've heard, engaging with the most thoughtful argument that side actually makes leads to a much stronger, more honest debate.

slides.title: Separating feelings from facts
slides.text: Recognizing when a strong emotional reaction — anger, excitement, fear — might be clouding a decision helps you think more clearly under pressure. For example, feeling furious after reading one upsetting headline might push you to share it immediately, but pausing to check the facts first, once the initial anger fades, often changes how you'd respond to it.

slides.title: Recognizing propaganda
slides.text: Propaganda uses one-sided, emotionally charged messaging to push a viewpoint rather than inform. Learning to notice it helps you separate persuasion from honest information. For example, a message using only scary language and dramatic music to push one specific opinion, while ignoring any counter-evidence entirely, is a sign you might be looking at propaganda rather than balanced information.

slides.title: The scientific method, briefly
slides.text: Form a question, propose an explanation, test it, and revise based on results — this basic loop underlies careful thinking far beyond just science class. For example, if you wonder "does studying with music help or hurt my focus," you could test it by studying with music some days and without on others, then honestly comparing your results — the same basic loop scientists use.

slides.title: Use your words
slides.text: When you feel happy, sad, or upset, saying it out loud with words helps people understand you better than yelling or crying alone. For example, saying "I'm sad because my tower fell down" helps a grown-up understand exactly what happened and how to help, much more than just crying without explaining why.

slides.title: Listening matters too
slides.text: Talking is only half of communicating — really listening when someone else is talking is just as important. For example, if your friend is telling you an exciting story about their weekend, looking at them and really paying attention shows them you care about what they're saying.

slides.title: "Please" and "thank you"
slides.text: Saying please when you ask for something, and thank you when someone helps you, makes people happy to help you again. For example, saying "can I have a snack, please?" instead of just demanding one, and saying "thank you" afterward, makes a grown-up much more willing to help you again next time.

slides.title: Asking for help
slides.text: If you're stuck or need something, asking for help with your words is a strong, smart thing to do — not something to feel bad about. For example, if you can't reach a toy on a high shelf, saying "can you help me reach this, please?" is much smarter than just standing there upset or trying to climb something dangerous.

slides.title: Your face says a lot too
slides.text: A smile, a frown, or wide eyes all send a message, even before you say a single word. For example, if you walk into a room smiling, people might guess you're happy about something even before you tell them what happened.

slides.title: Taking turns talking
slides.text: Waiting for your turn to talk — instead of interrupting — helps everyone feel heard in a conversation. For example, if two friends are talking and you want to share something, waiting until they finish their sentence before speaking helps everyone feel like they got a fair turn.

slides.title: Naming your feelings
slides.text: Words like happy, sad, mad, and scared help you tell someone exactly what's going on inside you, instead of just crying or shouting. For example, instead of just crying when a friend takes your toy, saying "I feel mad because you took my toy without asking" tells them exactly what's wrong and why.

slides.title: Showing what you mean
slides.text: If you can't find the words, pointing, drawing, or acting something out can help someone understand you too. For example, if you don't know the word for "the thing that spins on the ceiling," pointing up at the fan and moving your finger in a circle can help someone figure out exactly what you mean.

quiz.explanation: Showing what you mean is a great backup when words are hard to find.

slides.title: What is active listening?
slides.text: Active listening means really paying attention — looking at the person, not interrupting, and thinking about what they're saying instead of just waiting for your turn to talk. For example, if a friend is explaining a new game's rules, nodding along and asking a question about a part you didn't understand shows you're really listening, not just waiting to talk about your own idea.

slides.title: Body language basics
slides.text: Crossed arms, a big smile, or looking away all send messages without any words — noticing body language helps you understand people better. For example, if a friend says "I'm fine" but has crossed arms and won't look at you, their body language might be telling you something their words aren't.

slides.title: Taking turns in conversation
slides.text: A good conversation feels like a back-and-forth game of catch, not one person talking the whole time. For example, if you talk about your weekend for a full five minutes without asking your friend anything about theirs, the conversation stops feeling like catch and starts feeling one-sided.

slides.title: Disagreeing politely
slides.text: You can disagree with someone without being mean — saying 'I see it differently' is a respectful way to share a different opinion. For example, if a friend says a movie was the best ever and you didn't love it, saying "I see it differently — I thought the ending was a bit slow" keeps the conversation friendly instead of turning it into an argument.

slides.title: Asking clarifying questions
slides.text: If you don't understand something someone said, asking 'can you explain that again?' is smarter than just pretending to understand. For example, if a teacher explains a math step quickly and you're lost, asking "can you show that step again?" gets you the help you actually need instead of staying confused.

slides.title: Written vs. spoken words
slides.text: Writing a message and saying it out loud can feel very different — a text can sometimes sound different than you meant it to. For example, texting "fine" after a friend asks how you're doing can sound annoyed even if you just meant "okay" — saying the same word out loud with a smile would sound completely different.

slides.title: Checking in on feelings
slides.text: Asking a friend 'are you okay?' when they seem upset shows you're paying attention to more than just what they're saying. For example, if a friend seems quiet and isn't smiling at lunch, asking "hey, are you okay?" shows you noticed something was off, even before they said a word about it.

slides.title: Talking on the phone
slides.text: Without seeing someone's face, a phone call relies entirely on your voice and words — speaking clearly and listening closely both matter even more. For example, on a phone call you can't see a confused look on someone's face, so checking "does that make sense?" out loud matters more than it would in person.

slides.title: Comforting a sad friend
slides.text: Sometimes a friend doesn't need advice right away — just having someone sit with them and say 'that sounds really hard' can mean a lot. For example, if a friend's pet is sick and they're upset, simply sitting with them and saying "that sounds really hard, I'm sorry" often helps more than immediately jumping in with advice on what to do.

choices: Really paying attention instead of just waiting to talk
Talking as much as possible
quiz.explanation: Active listening means genuinely focusing on what the other person is saying.

choices: They might not actually be fine
Body language never means anything
quiz.explanation: Body language often communicates feelings just as clearly as words do.

choices: A back-and-forth, like a game of catch
One person talking the whole time
quiz.explanation: Good conversations involve both people talking and listening in turn.

slides.title: Knowing your audience
slides.text: How you explain something to a younger sibling is different from how you'd explain it to a teacher — good communicators adjust to who they're talking to. For example, explaining a video game's rules to a 5-year-old sibling might use simple words and lots of patience, while explaining the same rules to a teacher for a project might use more precise, detailed language.

slides.title: Persuasive communication
slides.text: Persuading someone works best with clear reasons and evidence, not just repeating what you want louder. For example, asking a parent for a later bedtime by saying "can I stay up later, please, please, please" is much weaker than explaining "I finish my homework by 8, and an extra 30 minutes would let me read before bed" with a real reason behind it.

slides.title: Reading tone in messages
slides.text: A short text like 'fine.' can come across as annoyed even if it wasn't meant that way — being aware of this helps avoid mixed-up messages. For example, texting just "k" in response to a friend's exciting news might come across as dismissive, even if you were just typing quickly and meant nothing by it.

slides.title: Giving feedback kindly
slides.text: Good feedback focuses on the specific thing that could improve, said kindly — not a vague or harsh comment about the person. For example, saying "the intro was a little confusing, maybe start with your main point first" helps a group project partner improve, while "this is bad" just makes them feel criticized without knowing what to fix.

slides.title: Receiving feedback well
slides.text: Hearing feedback about something you did isn't the same as being told you're a bad person — separating the two helps you actually improve. For example, if a teacher says your essay's conclusion needs work, that's feedback about one part of your writing, not a judgment about your intelligence or worth as a person.

slides.title: Resolving a disagreement
slides.text: Calmly explaining your side, actually listening to theirs, and looking for a solution both people can accept usually works better than arguing to 'win.' For example, if you and a sibling disagree about which show to watch, calmly explaining why you want your choice, listening to their reason, and maybe agreeing to alternate shows usually ends better than a shouting match over the remote.

slides.title: Written communication skills
slides.text: A clear, organized message — like a well-written email or message — gets read and understood much more easily than a rushed, jumbled one. For example, a message that says "Hi Coach, I'll miss practice Tuesday for a dentist appointment. See you Thursday!" gets a much faster, clearer response than a rambling message that buries that same information in the middle.

slides.title: Speaking up in a group
slides.text: Sharing your idea in front of a group takes practice. Preparing what you want to say ahead of time makes it feel much less intimidating. For example, jotting down two or three key points before a group discussion means you won't freeze up trying to remember what you wanted to say when it's your turn.

slides.title: Writing a clear message
slides.text: A short, well-organized message — saying exactly what you need and by when — gets a faster, better response than a vague, rambling one. For example, "Can you send me the group project notes by Thursday? I want to start my part this weekend" gets a much clearer response than just "hey, can you send me stuff sometime?"

slides.title: Public speaking basics
slides.text: Speaking to a group feels easier with preparation: knowing your key points, practicing out loud, and remembering that some nerves are completely normal. For example, practicing a class presentation out loud three times beforehand — even alone in your room — makes an enormous difference in how confident you sound on the actual day.

slides.title: Assertive vs. passive vs. aggressive
slides.text: Assertive communication states your needs clearly and respectfully. Passive avoids saying what you need. Aggressive disregards the other person's feelings entirely. For example, if a group project partner isn't doing their share, saying "I need you to finish your part by Friday so we're not scrambling" is assertive — staying silent and hoping it fixes itself is passive, and yelling "you never do anything" is aggressive.

slides.title: Conflict resolution
slides.text: Resolving conflict well usually means naming the real issue calmly, listening fully to the other side, and working toward a solution instead of assigning blame. For example, instead of saying "you always ignore me," naming the specific issue — "I felt left out when the group made plans without me" — opens the door to an actual conversation instead of a defensive reaction.

slides.title: Professional communication
slides.text: A clear subject line, a polite tone, and getting to the point efficiently make emails and messages far more effective in school or work settings. For example, an email titled "Question about Friday's assignment deadline" with two clear sentences gets answered far faster than one titled "hi" with a long, unfocused paragraph.

slides.title: Digital communication etiquette
slides.text: What you'd never say to someone's face shouldn't be said online either — screenshots and messages tend to stick around far longer than a spoken conversation. For example, a harsh comment typed in frustration can be screenshotted and shared long after you've cooled down and moved past the moment — something a spoken argument doesn't leave behind.

slides.title: Listening for understanding, not rebuttal
slides.text: Truly listening means trying to understand the other person's point, not just waiting for your turn to argue back. For example, in a disagreement about curfew, really listening to why a parent is worried (not just waiting to counter-argue) might reveal a specific concern you could actually address directly.

slides.title: Communicating across differences
slides.text: People from different backgrounds may communicate in different styles — being aware of this helps avoid misreading someone's tone or intent. For example, someone raised in a culture that values indirect communication might phrase a disagreement much more softly than someone used to being very direct — neither is wrong, but misreading the difference can cause unnecessary friction.

slides.title: Nonverbal cues under pressure
slides.text: In a tense conversation, tone of voice and body language often carry as much meaning as the actual words being said. For example, saying "I'm not mad" through gritted teeth and crossed arms sends a very different message than the actual words — the tone and body language often reveal more truth than the sentence itself.

slides.title: Communicating across cultures online
slides.text: Humor, directness, and formality norms vary a lot between cultures — a message that reads as friendly in one context can read as blunt or confusing in another. For example, a very short, direct message that feels efficient and normal in one culture's messaging style might come across as cold or rude to someone from a culture where messages are typically warmer and more elaborate.

slides.title: Introducing yourself professionally
slides.text: A short, confident self-introduction — your name, what you're interested in, and why you're reaching out — makes a strong first impression in interviews or networking. For example, "Hi, I'm Jordan, a junior interested in environmental science, and I'm reaching out because I'd love to learn more about your research" makes a far stronger first impression than a vague, rambling introduction.

slides.title: Some things stay private
slides.text: Your full name, address, and phone number are private — they're only for you and your family to know, not for sharing on a screen. For example, if a game asks "what's your address?" the answer is always to ask a grown-up first, never to type it in yourself.

slides.title: Always with a grown-up
slides.text: Using a tablet, phone, or computer with a grown-up nearby helps keep you safe while you explore and learn. For example, watching videos or playing a game while a parent is in the same room means someone is right there to help if something confusing or unexpected pops up.

slides.title: If something feels weird
slides.text: If anything on a screen makes you feel confused, scared, or uncomfortable, telling a grown-up right away is always the right choice. For example, if a video suddenly shows something scary or a game asks a strange question, walking away and telling a grown-up immediately is exactly the right move.

slides.title: Not everyone is who they say
slides.text: Someone online might not actually be who their picture or name says they are — that's why grown-ups help keep an eye on things. For example, an account with a picture of a kid might actually be run by someone much older pretending to be a kid, which is why chatting with strangers online always needs a grown-up's help.

slides.title: Ask before you click
slides.text: Before clicking on a button, a game, or a pop-up you don't recognize, it's smart to ask a grown-up first. For example, if a big flashing button suddenly appears saying "click here now!", that's exactly the kind of surprising pop-up to ask a grown-up about before clicking.

slides.title: Screens need breaks too
slides.text: Taking breaks from screens to play, read, or rest is part of staying healthy and happy. For example, after 30 minutes of watching a show, getting up to play outside or read a book for a while gives your eyes and body a healthy break.

slides.title: Pictures can be shared forever
slides.text: A picture you post can be saved or shared by others, even ones you didn't expect — so it's smart to only share pictures a grown-up says are okay. For example, a silly photo shared with one friend could get saved and passed along to other people you never intended to see it, which is why checking with a grown-up first matters.

slides.title: Only trusted apps and games
slides.text: Grown-ups check that an app or game is actually safe before you use it — that's why you should only use ones they've said are okay. For example, before downloading a new game a friend told you about, checking with a grown-up first helps make sure it's actually safe and appropriate.

slides.title: What makes a password strong?
slides.text: A strong password is hard for others to guess — not something simple like '123456' or your pet's name that everyone already knows. For example, a password like "BlueTiger$7Jump" is much harder to guess than "password123" or your dog's name, which anyone who knows you could figure out.

slides.title: Privacy settings
slides.text: Many apps let you choose who can see what you post — keeping things visible only to people you actually know is a smart default. For example, setting a photo-sharing app so only approved friends can see your posts, instead of "everyone," means strangers can't see what you're sharing.

slides.title: Stranger danger applies online too
slides.text: Just like you wouldn't share personal details with a stranger in person, you shouldn't share them with strangers online either. For example, if someone you've never met in real life asks what school you go to over a game chat, that's the same as a stranger asking you that question on the street — the answer is the same: don't share it.

slides.title: Being kind online
slides.text: Mean comments or messages hurt just as much online as they do in person — being kind matters everywhere. For example, typing a mean comment about someone's video feels easier from behind a screen, but it can hurt just as much as saying it to their face — so the same kindness rules apply.

slides.title: What to do about unkindness
slides.text: If someone is mean to you online, telling a grown-up and not responding with more meanness is the safest, smartest choice. For example, if someone leaves a rude comment on something you posted, screenshotting it and showing a grown-up is much smarter than firing back an even meaner comment.

slides.title: Careful with downloads
slides.text: Not every game, app, or file is safe to download — checking with a grown-up before downloading something new is a good habit. For example, a message saying "download this free game mod" from an unfamiliar website could actually contain something harmful, which is exactly why checking with a grown-up first matters.

slides.title: Checking if a link is safe
slides.text: A message saying 'click here to win a prize!' from someone you don't know is usually a trick, not a real prize. For example, a pop-up claiming "you've won a free gaming console, click here!" is almost always a scam trying to trick you into giving up information, not a real prize.

slides.title: Chatting in online games
slides.text: Some games let you chat with other players you don't know in real life. Keep personal details out of game chats, just like anywhere else online. For example, if a player in your online game asks "what city do you live in?", the safe answer is to not share that, the same way you wouldn't tell a stranger at the park.

slides.title: In-app purchases need a grown-up
slides.text: Buying extra coins, skins, or upgrades inside a game usually costs real money — always check with a grown-up before buying anything. For example, a game button that says "buy 500 coins for $4.99" is spending real money from a real credit card, even though it feels like just clicking a button in a game.

slides.title: What is phishing?
slides.text: Phishing is a trick where a fake message pretends to be from someone trustworthy (like a game company) to try to steal your password or personal information. For example, an email that looks like it's from a game company saying "your account will be deleted, click here to verify your password" is a classic phishing attempt designed to steal your login.

slides.title: Oversharing online
slides.text: Posting your location, school name, or daily schedule can reveal more about you to strangers than you might realize. For example, a post saying "at soccer practice every Tuesday at 4pm at Central Park" tells any stranger exactly where to find you at a specific, predictable time — far more than most people would say out loud to someone they don't know.

slides.title: Your digital footprint
slides.text: Everything you post, like, or comment online adds up over time into a 'digital footprint' — a trail that can be seen by others, even years later. For example, comments and photos posted at age 12 can still be found by someone searching your name years later, which is why it's worth thinking about before posting.

slides.title: Balancing screen time
slides.text: Noticing when screen time is crowding out sleep, friends, or activities you enjoy is an important digital safety and wellbeing skill. For example, if staying up late scrolling means you're too tired to enjoy soccer practice the next day, that's a sign screen time might need rebalancing.

slides.title: Fake accounts and catfishing
slides.text: Someone online might use a fake photo and name to pretend to be someone they're not — this is sometimes called 'catfishing.' For example, an account claiming to be a 13-year-old with a cute profile photo could actually belong to a much older adult using a stolen or fake picture — which is why meeting an online-only friend in person always needs a trusted adult involved.

slides.title: Two-factor authentication
slides.text: Some accounts offer an extra security step — like a code sent to your phone — on top of your password. It's an easy way to make an account harder to break into. For example, even if someone guessed or stole your password, two-factor authentication means they'd also need the one-time code sent to your phone, which they wouldn't have.

slides.title: When to disengage and report
slides.text: If an online conversation starts feeling uncomfortable or pressuring, stopping the conversation and reporting or telling a trusted adult is always okay. For example, if someone online keeps pushing you to share a photo or secret you don't want to share, ending the conversation and telling a trusted adult right away is the right call, no matter what they said to try to stop you.

slides.title: Location sharing risks
slides.text: Live location sharing can be useful with close family, but sharing it publicly or with people you barely know can reveal exactly where you are, in real time. For example, sharing your live location with a parent so they know you got to a friend's house safely makes sense, but sharing that same live location publicly means literally anyone could see exactly where you are right now.

slides.title: Online friends vs. real friends
slides.text: Someone you've only ever talked to online is different from a friend you actually know in person — it's wise to be more cautious about what you share and trust. For example, an online gaming friend you've chatted with for months might seem trustworthy, but since you've never actually met them in person, it makes sense to be more careful about what personal details you share with them.
